currency_note: IMPORTANT: Canadian National Railway reports its financial statements in CANADIAN DOLLARS (CAD), not USD. CN is a Canadian foreign private issuer that files Form 40-F (Canadian MJDS annual report) with the SEC rather than a 10-K, and its primary listing is the TSX (ticker CNR.TO) with a secondary NYSE listing (ticker CNI). All revenue, income, balance sheet and per-share figures discussed below are CAD unless explicitly noted otherwise. NOTE: the extracted core_metrics table / CNI_Metrics.csv in this research folder currently mislabels the currency column as 'USD' due to a known bug in build_facts_xbrl.py, which hardcodes USD regardless of the actual XBRL unit tag. The underlying dollar figures are genuinely CAD-denominated and should be treated as such by any downstream DCF or cross-ticker comparison.
overview: Canadian National Railway (CN) is a Class I freight railway headquartered in Montreal, Quebec, operating a roughly 20,000-mile network that is the only rail system spanning Canada coast-to-coast (Atlantic to Pacific) with a direct line to the U.S. Gulf Coast, giving it single-line access to three coasts. CN moves more than 300 million tons of natural resources, manufactured products and finished goods annually across Canada and the U.S. Midwest/South, generating roughly C$17.3 billion in 2025 revenue. It is dual-listed, with its primary listing on the TSX (CNR.TO) and a secondary listing on the NYSE (CNI), and files a Form 40-F annual report with the SEC under the U.S.-Canada Multijurisdictional Disclosure System (MJDS) rather than a 10-K.

business_model.summary: CN generates revenue by hauling freight for shippers under a mix of contract and tariff-based pricing across seven major commodity groups, moving diversified bulk, merchandise and intermodal traffic across a uniquely diversified single-line network connecting the Atlantic, Pacific and Gulf coasts. Revenue is largely volume- and price-driven (carloads/containers x revenue per unit), not subscription-based, but demand is diversified across many end markets (agriculture, energy, forestry, manufacturing, retail/consumer) which smooths single-commodity cyclicality somewhat. Pricing has inflation-plus characteristics due to limited competitive alternatives on much of the network (effectively a regulated/duopoly pricing environment subject to Canadian Transportation Agency and U.S. Surface Transportation Board oversight).
business_model.customer_type: B2B — shippers, freight forwarders, grain handlers, energy and chemical producers, forest-products companies, automakers, and intermodal/logistics companies (steamship lines, trucking partners); no direct B2C exposure
business_model.geographic_mix: Network spans Canada (Atlantic to Pacific) and the U.S. Midwest/Gulf Coast via subsidiaries (Illinois Central, Wisconsin Central, Grand Trunk Corporation, and the former EJ&E); approximately 32% of total revenue is tied to Canada-U.S. cross-border traffic; reporting currency is CAD with meaningful USD-denominated revenue and costs on U.S. operations creating FX translation exposure

main_competitors: Canadian Pacific Kansas City (CPKC) — the only other Canadian Class I, now with a unique single-line Canada-U.S.-Mexico network post CP-Kansas City Southern merger
Union Pacific (UP) and BNSF — U.S. Class I railroads that interchange with/compete indirectly for cross-border traffic
CSX and Norfolk Southern — eastern U.S. Class I railroads relevant to interline and intermodal competition
Trucking companies (long-haul for-hire carriers) — compete for shorter-haul, higher-value, time-sensitive freight
Marine/barge and pipeline operators — alternative modes for bulk commodities (notably petroleum)
competitive_position.market_position: One of two Class I railways in Canada (effective duopoly with CPKC); CN is the larger of the two Canadian carriers by revenue and route-miles, and is the only railway with single-line service connecting the Atlantic, Pacific and Gulf of Mexico coasts, a structural differentiator even versus CPKC's new north-south Mexico reach.

moat_factors.description: Irreplaceable physical rail network (right-of-way, track, yards) built over 100+ years; nearly impossible to replicate given land acquisition, regulatory and capital barriers — a classic natural monopoly/duopoly characteristic.

Building a competing Class I network is not practically feasible given right-of-way scarcity, environmental approvals and capital intensity; effectively locks in a two-railroad market in most of Canada.

moat_factors.factor: High switching costs / lack of alternatives
moat_factors.description: Many shippers (grain elevators, mines, refineries, mills) are rail-captive with no practical trucking or pipeline alternative for the volumes and distances involved.

CN's unique Atlantic-Pacific-Gulf single-line network avoids costly interline handoffs other railroads must use, supporting service reliability and cost advantages on long-haul, multi-modal-competitive freight.

Precision Scheduled Railroading (PSR) operating model and fixed-cost network economics mean incremental volume carries high operating leverage, supporting industry-leading operating ratios historically.
Large, consistent capital program (~C$2.8-3.7B/year) funds double-tracking, sidings and technology that smaller/regional carriers cannot match, reinforcing service reliability.

weaknesses: Heavily unionized workforce (Teamsters Canada Rail Conference/TCRC and other crafts) creates periodic labor disruption risk, as shown by the August 2024 CN/CPKC simultaneous lockout that briefly halted both networks
Significant cross-border exposure (~32% of revenue) makes CN a direct conduit for U.S.-Canada tariff and trade-policy risk
Commodity concentration in cyclical bulk categories (grain, forest products, metals, coal, petroleum) exposes revenue to agricultural weather/harvest variability and industrial/commodity cycles
Regulated/quasi-regulated pricing environment (CTA in Canada, STB oversight on U.S. operations) limits full pricing power versus an unregulated business
High fixed-cost, capital-intensive network requires continuous heavy capex (~C$2.8-3.7B annually) regardless of volume cycle, pressuring free cash flow in downturns
FX translation risk given USD-denominated U.S. segment revenue/costs reported in CAD functional/presentation currency

growth_drivers: Intermodal growth — the largest and fastest-growing commodity category (22% of 2025 revenue), benefiting from truck-to-rail conversion, e-commerce logistics, and port/ports-of-entry growth on the West Coast (Prince Rupert) and Gulf
Grain and fertilizer volumes — structural demand growth tied to Canadian/U.S. agricultural exports and global food security, supported by CN's unique access to export terminals on multiple coasts
Energy-related traffic — crude-by-rail, refined products, and growing frac sand/LNG-linked chemical traffic as Canadian energy infrastructure (e.g., LNG Canada ramp-up) develops
Precision Scheduled Railroading (PSR) and continued operating efficiency gains — record fuel efficiency in H1 2026, falling operating ratio supporting margin expansion

Capital discipline and shareholder returns — 30 consecutive years of dividend increases, active share buybacks (up to 24 million shares/~3.9% of shares outstanding authorized Feb 2026-Feb 2027), reducing share count and supporting EPS growth

Technology/automation investment — continued deployment of advanced train control, automated inspection, and digital scheduling tools to support safety and throughput without proportional headcount growth
Potential further rail consolidation industry-wide (following CPKC's CP-KCS combination) could reshape competitive dynamics, though CN's own KCS bid failed in 2021

business.description: Grain, forest products, metals/minerals, and coal volumes are sensitive to harvests, weather, global commodity prices and industrial cycles; a broad slowdown in Canadian/U.S. industrial activity would reduce carloads.
No single customer dominates, but heavy reliance on cyclical bulk industries (energy, mining, agriculture, forestry) ties results to commodity cycles outside CN's control.

CPKC's new single-line Canada-U.S.-Mexico network (post Kansas City Southern merger) could divert some cross-border intermodal and merchandise traffic; trucking competes on shorter, higher-value lanes.

Wildfires, flooding, extreme winter weather, and infrastructure incidents (e.g., bridge/tunnel outages) can disrupt CN's single-line network with no easy rerouting alternative given limited parallel track.

financial.description: Total debt of ~C$22.1 billion against ~C$21.6 billion of shareholders' equity (FY2025); capital-intensive business requires continuous debt-funded capex and refinancing, exposing CN to interest-rate and credit-market conditions.

Significant U.S.-dollar-denominated revenue and costs from U.S. subsidiary operations (Illinois Central, Wisconsin Central, Grand Trunk) translated into CAD reporting currency create earnings volatility from CAD/USD exchange rate swings.
Capital spending of ~C$2.8-3.7 billion annually for track, bridges, equipment and safety is largely non-discretionary, constraining free cash flow flexibility in a downturn.

regulatory.description: Transport Canada and the U.S. FRA continue to tighten safety rules (train length, braking technology, hazardous-materials routing) following high-profile North American rail incidents (e.g., East Palestine, OH derailment on a peer railroad); compliance costs and potential operational restrictions (e.g., mandated crew-size rules) are an ongoing overhang.

The August 2024 simultaneous CN/CPKC lockout and TCRC strike notice — resolved via Canada Industrial Relations Board (CIRB) intervention and later binding arbitration (3%/year wage deal through Dec 2026) — illustrates recurring risk from Canada's unique labor-dispute framework; renegotiation is due again as the current TCRC agreement expires at the end of 2026.

Rate regulation, interswitching rules, and service-level obligations in Canada, plus U.S. Surface Transportation Board oversight of rates and mergers, constrain pricing power and could tighten further amid political pressure around rail 'monopoly' concerns (public commentary on breaking up the CN/CPKC duopoly persists).

regulatory.risk: Cross-border tariff and trade policy risk
regulatory.description: As of 2026, new U.S. tariffs of up to 50% on certain Canadian goods (effective August 2026) and retaliatory Canadian tariffs on U.S. imports directly threaten cross-border freight volumes; CN management has flagged trade-policy uncertainty as 'the biggest risk' to the business, given ~32% of revenue is tied to U.S.-Canada cross-border traffic. USMCA review adds further policy uncertainty.

macro.description: High fixed-asset base and ongoing debt issuance (including under a 2024 shelf prospectus) make CN sensitive to borrowing costs; however, long-dated debt maturities partially mitigate near-term refinancing risk.
A broad U.S./Canada recession or a poor grain harvest would directly reduce rail volumes across most commodity categories simultaneously.
Diesel fuel is a major input cost; fuel surcharge mechanisms in most contracts mitigate but do not fully eliminate the impact of oil price swings.
A stronger Canadian dollar reduces the CAD-translated value of U.S.-segment revenue and could pressure reported margins; a weaker CAD has the opposite effect.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: North American Class I rail volumes are expected to grow at low-single-digit rates longer term, with intermodal (truck-to-rail conversion) and energy/agricultural exports the strongest secular growth categories; the industry overall is mature and consolidated into seven Class I railroads (soon effectively six distinct networks post CPKC-KCS), with regulatory scrutiny of further consolidation very high.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate — diversified across bulk, merchandise and intermodal categories which smooths single-commodity swings, but still correlated with broad industrial production, agricultural output, energy activity and consumer goods movement; 2024-2025 showed a mild volume recovery after a soft 2023-2024 stretch.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate — capital-intensive business with continuous debt issuance for capex; rate increases raise financing costs on new/refinanced debt but existing long-dated debt provides some insulation.
macro_factors.currency_exposure: Reports in CAD; meaningful USD revenue/cost exposure from U.S. rail subsidiaries creates translation risk on CAD/USD moves; investors buying CNI on NYSE receive USD-quoted shares referencing a CAD-denominated business, so currency movements affect USD-equivalent returns independent of underlying CAD performance.
key_input_costs: Electricity/energy for yard and terminal operations

recent_developments.event: CN reported Q2 2026 revenue of C$4,753 million (+11% YoY), diluted EPS of C$2.06 (+10% YoY), adjusted diluted EPS of C$2.08 (+11% YoY); operating ratio 62.5% (up 80bps); revenue ton miles +5%; free cash flow for H1 2026 of C$1,842 million (+19% YoY); raised full-year 2026 guidance.

Management raised FY2026 guidance: revenue ton mile growth revised to 'low single-digit' (from 'flattish'), and adjusted diluted EPS growth revised to 'mid-to-high single-digit' (from 'slightly exceeding RTM growth'); FY2026 capex reaffirmed at approximately C$2.8 billion net of customer reimbursements.

CN reported FY2025 revenue of C$17.3 billion, net income of C$4.72 billion, EPS growth of 8%, improved operating ratio, and record free cash flow of ~C$3.34 billion; board raised the quarterly dividend 3% to C$0.915/share (30th consecutive annual increase) and approved a new share buyback authorizing repurchase of up to 24 million shares (~3.9% of shares outstanding) through February 2027.
FY2026 capex guidance set at approximately C$2.8 billion, down roughly C$500 million from 2025's ~C$3.7 billion, reflecting a step-down in major capacity projects and continued capital discipline.

Escalating U.S.-Canada tariff dispute: new U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods reported as high as 50% effective August 2026, with Canadian retaliatory tariffs on U.S. imports; CN has disclosed roughly C$350 million of revenue impact attributable to tariff-related uncertainty/trade disruption in early 2026, and management has characterized trade-policy uncertainty as the single biggest risk to the outlook; approximately 32% of CN's revenue is tied to U.S.-Canada cross-border traffic.

Binding arbitration concluded the CN-TCRC labor dispute stemming from the August 2024 mutual CN/CPKC lockout and strike notices (which briefly halted both railways); the resulting agreement provides for approximately 3% annual wage increases effective January 1, 2024 through December 31, 2026 (no union ratification required), removing near-term labor overhang through the remainder of 2026.

Revenue mix for 2025: Intermodal 22%, Grain & Fertilizers 23%, Petroleum & Chemicals 21%, Metals & Minerals 11%, Forest Products 10%, Automotive 5%, Coal 5%; Q4 2025 saw growth in most categories except grain/fertilizers (-3% YoY).

items.notes: Raised from prior guidance of 'flattish' growth following strong H1 2026 grain and energy volumes.
Raised from prior guidance of growth 'slightly exceeding RTM growth'; reflects operating leverage, buybacks and cost discipline.
Down roughly C$500 million from FY2025 actual capex of ~C$3.66 billion, reflecting completion of major capacity projects and continued capital discipline.
30th consecutive year of dividend increases, declared January 2026.

items.target: Up to 24 million shares (~3.9% of shares outstanding)
items.notes: New Normal Course Issuer Bid; ~3 million shares repurchased for C$454 million in Q2 2026 alone.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Tracy Robinson highlighted 'solid operational and commercial performance, improved productivity, strong cash flow generation, and continued financial discipline' in Q2 2026, citing record fuel efficiency and strong grain and energy volumes in H1 2026. Management has simultaneously flagged U.S.-Canada tariff and trade-policy uncertainty as the biggest risk to the outlook, estimating a roughly C$350 million revenue impact from tariff-related disruption, even as it raised full-year guidance on strength in base operations.

bull_case: Irreplaceable, century-old rail network with structural moat (duopoly with CPKC, single-line access to Atlantic, Pacific and Gulf coasts) that is effectively impossible for a new entrant to replicate
Diversified commodity mix (intermodal, grain, petrochemicals, metals, forest products, automotive, coal) smooths single-sector cyclicality versus commodity-pure-play peers

Consistent capital returns — 30 consecutive years of dividend increases plus an active, sizeable buyback program (up to ~3.9% of shares outstanding in the current authorization), supporting EPS growth independent of volume growth
Operating leverage from Precision Scheduled Railroading (PSR) and record fuel efficiency is driving margin expansion even amid tariff headwinds, as shown by the Q2 2026 beat-and-raise

Long-term secular tailwinds from truck-to-rail conversion in intermodal and growing Canadian energy/agricultural export volumes (e.g., LNG Canada ramp-up, grain export growth) support multi-year volume growth above GDP
bear_case: Direct, concentrated exposure to escalating U.S.-Canada tariff conflict — management itself has called trade-policy uncertainty the single biggest risk, with ~32% of revenue tied to cross-border traffic and a disclosed ~C$350 million revenue hit already absorbed in 2026

Recurring labor-relations risk under Canada's unique rail bargaining framework — the August 2024 CN/CPKC mutual lockout briefly halted the entire Canadian rail network, and the current TCRC wage agreement expires at the end of 2026, setting up another negotiation cycle
High leverage (~C$22 billion total debt) and continuous heavy sustaining capex (~C$2.8-3.7 billion/year) limit financial flexibility in a prolonged freight downturn or rate-rising environment

Regulatory and political pressure around the CN/CPKC 'rail duopoly' structure, plus CTA/STB oversight, caps pricing power and could tighten further amid public calls to break up Canadian rail monopolies

CAD-denominated reporting with meaningful USD-segment exposure creates earnings and USD-equivalent-return volatility for NYSE-listed (CNI) investors purely from currency translation, independent of underlying operating performance
